title: Italy
description: Twenty regions and hundreds of native grapes, read through the places that explain the rest.
L: Italy's system has DOCG at the top, with 77 wines, then DOC, then IGT, Indicazione Geografica Tipica, then Vino. DOCG wines must pass a tasting panel and carry a numbered strip on the neck. Italy has wine in all 20 regions and hundreds of native grapes, more than any other country.

In the 1970s, some Tuscan producers made wines with Cabernet Sauvignon or in small new barrels, which broke DOC rules. They had to sell them as simple table wine, yet charged more than any Chianti. These Super Tuscans, like Sassicaia and Tignanello, led to the IGT category in 1992, giving room for wines outside the rules.
Why was the IGT category created?
To give a home to quality wines outside DOC rules
Super Tuscans broke DOC rules, so IGT gave them, and similar wines, a proper category.

Classico marks the historic heart of a zone, like Chianti Classico or Soave Classico. Superiore usually means higher minimum alcohol and sometimes longer ageing. Riserva means longer minimum ageing, set for each wine; Barolo Riserva needs at least 62 months. These words have legal meaning in each DOC.
Classico: historic core. Riserva: longer ageing.
Order Italy's quality levels from highest to lowest.
DOCG is the strictest, Vino the most open.
Italy has DOCG, DOC, IGT and Vino
Super Tuscans led to the IGT category
Classico, Superiore and Riserva carry legal meaning
At the foot of the mountains

Piedmont means foot of the mountains, surrounded by the Alps on three sides. The climate is continental, with autumn fog. The best vineyards are on the Langhe and Roero hills around Alba, on calcareous marl. South-facing slopes are kept for Nebbiolo, which ripens last; others go to Barbera, Dolcetto or Moscato.
Langhe hills, fog, Nebbiolo on the best slopes

Barolo and Barbaresco are both 100% Nebbiolo DOCGs. Barolo must age at least 38 months, 18 in wood; Barbaresco at least 26 months, 9 in wood. Barbaresco is slightly warmer and lower, often a little earlier to approach. Since 2010, both list named vineyards, called MGA, such as Cannubi in Barolo.
What is the minimum total ageing for Barolo?
Barolo needs 38 months, including 18 in wood. 62 months is for Barolo Riserva; 26 for Barbaresco.

Barbera is Piedmont's most planted red: deep colour, high acidity, low tannin, often from Asti or Alba. Dolcetto is softer and earlier-drinking, with dark fruit and bitter almond. Moscato Bianco makes Asti and Moscato d'Asti. In the Roero, Arneis is a fragrant white; in the south-east, Gavi is made from Cortese.
Match each grape to its typical character.
Piedmont's grapes divide the hills by ripening time.
Piedmont's best slopes, in the Langhe, go to Nebbiolo
Barolo and Barbaresco are 100% Nebbiolo with long ageing
Barbera, Dolcetto, Moscato, Arneis and Cortese fill out the region
Explain how the Alps shape the north-east

The Veneto makes more wine than almost any other Italian region. Valpolicella, near Verona, uses Corvina for light reds, Ripasso and Amarone. Soave, east of Verona, uses Garganega. Prosecco is made from Glera across the Veneto and Friuli. Lake Garda tempers the western side, where Bardolino and Lugana grow.

The Alps protect the north-east from cold northern winds, while their cool air flows down valleys at night, keeping acidity high. In Alto Adige, vineyards climb from 200 to over 1,000 m, growing Pinot Grigio, Gewürztraminer and the red Lagrein. Friuli, near Slovenia, makes crisp whites from Friulano, Pinot Grigio and Ribolla Gialla.
Mountain air keeps the wines fresh
Match each wine to its region.
Each north-eastern region has its own grapes.

In Friuli, near the Slovenian border, producers like Josko Gravner revived long skin contact for white grapes in the 1990s, sometimes in Georgian qvevri. Ribolla Gialla and Friulano became amber, tannic wines. Friuli's Collio and Colli Orientali are now reference areas for this style, alongside Slovenia's Brda.
Friuli: home of modern orange wine
Alto Adige has vineyards above 1,000 metres.
Yes. Its mountain vineyards climb from about 200 m to over 1,000 m, keeping wines fresh and aromatic.
The Veneto makes Valpolicella, Soave and Prosecco
The Alps keep Alto Adige and Friuli fresh
Friuli is a reference for modern orange wine

Chianti covers a wide area between Florence and Siena. Chianti Classico is the historic heart, with its black rooster symbol; it's a separate DOCG and must be at least 80% Sangiovese. Since 2014, Gran Selezione sits at the top, from estate grapes with longer ageing. Galestro and alberese soils, rocky marl and limestone, give the best wines.

Brunello di Montalcino, south of Siena, is 100% Sangiovese, warmer and drier, with at least five years of ageing, two in oak. Vino Nobile di Montepulciano, from a different hill town, must be at least 70% Sangiovese, called Prugnolo Gentile there. It's not the same as Montepulciano d'Abruzzo, which is a grape and a different region.
A wine from the Montepulciano grape, in Abruzzo
Montepulciano d'Abruzzo is made from the Montepulciano grape in Abruzzo. Vino Nobile di Montepulciano is Sangiovese from the Tuscan town.

On Tuscany's coast, Bolgheri became famous with Sassicaia, first sold in 1971, made from Cabernet Sauvignon. Bordeaux grapes thrive in the warm, maritime conditions. Bolgheri DOC now covers these blends, and Sassicaia has its own DOC. Inland, Tignanello blended Sangiovese with Cabernet.
Bolgheri: Bordeaux grapes on the coast
Which wines are based on Sangiovese?
Chianti Classico is the historic heart, at least 80% Sangiovese
Brunello is 100% Sangiovese; Vino Nobile at least 70%
Bolgheri grows Bordeaux grapes on the coast
Describe the main wines of central Italy
Name key grapes of the Adriatic coast
Explain the role of Verdicchio and Montepulciano

On the Adriatic coast, Marche and Abruzzo dominate. Marche's Verdicchio, from Castelli di Jesi and Matelica, gives crisp, almond-scented whites that can age well. Abruzzo's Montepulciano gives deep, soft, plummy reds, and its rosé is called Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo. Conero, near Ancona, makes structured Montepulciano reds.

Umbria, landlocked, has Orvieto, a white blend led by Grechetto and Trebbiano, and Montefalco Sagrantino, one of the most tannic red grapes in the world. Lazio, around Rome, is known for Frascati, a light white from Malvasia and Trebbiano. Altitude and volcanic soils help keep these wines fresh.
Match each wine to its region.
Central Italy offers distinct wines on both sides of the Apennines.
Verdicchio is one of Italy's best-value whites. Good ones, like Castelli di Jesi Riserva, gain honey and almond notes with five years in bottle.
Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo is a rosé made from the ____ grape.
Montepulciano's deep colour gives Cerasuolo its cherry-red hue.
Marche's Verdicchio is a crisp, age-worthy white
Abruzzo's Montepulciano gives soft reds and Cerasuolo rosé
Umbria has Sagrantino and Orvieto; Lazio has Frascati
Describe the main wines of Campania
Explain why volcanic soils matter in the south

Campania, around Naples, grows ancient grapes. Aglianico makes Taurasi, a powerful, tannic red often called the Barolo of the south. Fiano di Avellino and Greco di Tufo are DOCG whites, nutty and mineral. Vesuvius and the inland hills have volcanic soils, which drain well and resisted phylloxera in places.

Puglia, the heel of Italy, is hot, flat and productive. Primitivo, the same grape as Zinfandel, gives ripe, high-alcohol reds, especially in Manduria. Negroamaro makes reds and rosés in Salento. In Basilicata, Aglianico del Vulture grows on the slopes of an extinct volcano, at up to 800 m, giving fresher Aglianico.
Taurasi is Campania's DOCG Aglianico, structured and long-lived.

The south is hot, so the best wines come from altitude, sea breezes or volcanic slopes. Irpinia's vineyards, for Taurasi and Fiano, reach 400 to 700 m. Volcanic soils also give a distinctive savoury, smoky edge, and often ungrafted old vines.
Altitude and volcanoes temper the heat
Primitivo di Manduria comes from Puglia.
Campania's Aglianico makes Taurasi; Fiano and Greco are its whites
Altitude and volcanic soils give freshness in the hot south
Describe Sicily's key grapes and areas

Sicily is Italy's largest island and one of its largest wine regions. Nero d'Avola is its signature red, dark and ripe. Grillo and Catarratto are its main whites, once used for Marsala, the fortified wine of the west. Since 2011, the Sicilia DOC covers the whole island, and Cerasuolo di Vittoria is its only DOCG.

Mount Etna is an active volcano, with vineyards from 400 to over 1,000 m. Altitude gives cool nights, and black volcanic soils, often with ungrafted old vines, give fine, savoury wines. Nerello Mascalese makes pale, elegant reds often compared with Pinot Noir and Nebbiolo; Carricante makes taut, citrus whites. Etna was among Italy's first DOCs, in 1968.
Etna's reds are mainly made from Nero d'Avola.
Not true. Etna's reds are based on Nerello Mascalese, a paler, more elegant grape. Nero d'Avola belongs to the warmer south-east.

Sardinia's wines show Spanish influence from centuries of rule. Cannonau is Grenache, giving ripe, warm reds. Vermentino di Gallura, the island's only DOCG, is a crisp, salty white from granite soils in the north-east. Carignano del Sulcis comes from old Carignan vines near the sea.
Match each grape to its island.
Each island has grapes shaped by its history.
Sicily grows Nero d'Avola, Grillo and Catarratto
Etna's altitude gives fine Nerello Mascalese and Carricante
Sardinia's Cannonau is Grenache; Vermentino di Gallura its DOCG
Link Italy's regions to their grapes
Match each wine to its grape.
Italy's great wines are made from native grapes.
What led to the creation of the IGT category?
Super Tuscans made great wines outside DOC rules.
Vino Nobile di Montepulciano is made from the Montepulciano grape.
Not true. It's made mostly from Sangiovese in the Tuscan town of Montepulciano.
Etna's main red grape is Nerello ____.
Nerello Mascalese gives Etna's pale, elegant reds.
DOCG, DOC, IGT and Vino rank Italian wine
Piedmont and Tuscany lead with Nebbiolo and Sangiovese
The north-east is fresh and Alpine; the south is volcanic and warm
Italy's strength is its hundreds of native grapes
